AI workflow orchestration · case study

How an AI workflow turned a finance brief into a testable product experience.

Smart Expense Tracker is a complete UX orchestration case study: evidence enters first, specialized AI work happens in bounded phases, and people retain the decision at every review gate.

The operating principles

AI can accelerate the work. It cannot inherit accountability.

01 · SOURCE

Evidence enters before synthesis.

BRD constraints and project artefacts form the truth set. Missing details remain open questions rather than invented “facts.”

02 · WORK

Jobs are deliberately bounded.

Each skill defines its inputs, method, expected output, validation checks and a clear stopping condition.

03 · DECISION

Approval stays human.

The orchestrator routes work, but only an explicit APPROVE, REVISE or REJECT can move a gate.

Workflow at a glance

A controlled path from ambiguity to validated design.

The workflow is designed as a sequence of narrow, inspectable handoffs. Every phase leaves behind artifacts that become the permitted inputs for the next one.

01DiscoverResearch the evidence
G1ReviewHuman research gate
02DefineFrame the problem
G2ReviewRequirements gate
03–05Make it realDevelop, deliver, build
G3–G5ReviewInspect each handoff
06ValidateRelease-readiness gate
The six-phase cycle

Each phase has one job, one accountable agent, and named deliverables.

01Discover agent

Understand the evidence.

Turns the provided brief into a defensible picture of users, problems, market context and journey friction.

  • Problem exploration
  • Competitive audit
  • Interview scripts
  • Journey map
→ D1 human review
02Define agent

Frame the right problem.

Separates known evidence from assumptions, creates personas, scopes features and writes formal requirements.

  • Problem statement
  • User personas
  • Feature matrix
  • UX requirements
→ D2 human review
03Develop agent

Shape the experience.

Translates approved scope into navigation, flows, structural concepts and wireframe specifications.

  • Design concepts
  • Information architecture
  • User flows
  • Wireframes
→ D3 human review
04Deliver agent

Define the visual system.

Creates UI specifications, DTCG tokens, clear product microcopy and a developer-facing handoff.

  • UI specifications
  • Design tokens
  • UX copy guide
  • Developer handoff
→ D4 human review
05Build agent

Prepare implementation.

Maps the design system to components, typed interfaces, code snippets and a prototype state model.

  • Component library
  • Code snippets
  • System config
  • Prototype guide
→ D5 human review
06Validation agent

Check the outcome.

Records static usability, accessibility, heuristic and design-QA evidence, including what remains unverified.

  • Usability protocol
  • Accessibility audit
  • Heuristic review
  • Design QA log
→ D6 release handoff
The skill catalogue

Twenty-four repeatable methods make the agents useful.

An agent is not a single all-purpose prompt. It coordinates four narrowly defined skills: each with evidence boundaries, a repeatable method, expected deliverables and a stopping condition.

How the orchestrator works

It decides what may happen next, not what should be approved.

The orchestrator reads the current project state, verifies prerequisites, selects the only permitted phase, and stops whenever a human decision is required.

IF Phase 01 outputs are complete → request D1 review IF D1 is explicitly APPROVE → dispatch Define agent IF reviewer requests REVISE → rerun the affected skill + downstream dependencies IF reviewer selects REJECT → halt the workflow
How to use the structure

Choose a controlled mode, then run only what that mode permits.

Start from approved inputs

Place the BRD and cleared research in the input area. Run Discover, inspect D1, then advance one approved phase at a time. This is the safest choice for a new product.

Use it when

You need end-to-end traceability and have not yet approved a later phase.

Request:
"Start the Smart Expense Tracker workflow.
Read the orchestrator, determine the current
state, and run only the next permitted phase.
Stop for every human gate."

Run one bounded piece of work

Use a single phase only when its exact prerequisite artefacts are present and the preceding gate was explicitly approved.

Use it when

You are improving one phase without claiming to have completed the full route.

Request:
"Run Phase 03 only. Verify D2 approval and
read only the named Phase 02 inputs. Create
the declared Phase 03 outputs and stop at D3."

Correct without restarting everything

Identify the review finding, rerun its affected skill, then regenerate only downstream work that now depends on it. Return to the same gate for a new decision.

Use it when

A reviewer requests a change, or evidence invalidates a specific artefact.

Request:
"Revise D4 feedback on interaction states.
Rerun the affected delivery skill and only its
dependent outputs. Keep earlier approved
artefacts and return to D4 review."

Continue from a valid stopping point

Read the review records, identify the last approved gate, validate that the required artefacts still match, then run the next permitted phase.

Use it when

The workflow paused between sessions or a project is being handed to a new team member.

Request:
"Resume this project. Inspect review records,
confirm the last valid approval, report the
next allowed phase, then run it only if all
entry criteria are satisfied."
The review contract

Readiness is not approval.

Automated work may produce a complete package. It cannot silently promote that package to the next phase. The human gate keeps the workflow inspectable and accountable.

APPROVE

Advance the route

The named artefacts are accepted at their current version. The next phase becomes eligible.

REVISE

Return to the cause

Feedback identifies an affected skill. Only that work and its dependent outputs are regenerated.

REJECT

Stop the route

The workflow halts. It does not infer a workaround, a new scope or a release decision.

A practical starting point

Build your own AI workflow one accountable layer at a time.

01

Start with a small output

Define the result and approved inputs first. “Create a budget flow from these requirements” is actionable; “design my entire product” is not.

02

Write a skill before you write an agent

Make one repeatable method with a source boundary, ordered process, expected output and quality check.

03

Group skills under a phase lead

An agent coordinates related skills but stays within the phase contract and its declared outputs.

04

Put a human gate after every phase

Bind the review to specific artefacts and never treat a lack of objection as approval.
